paras: The lynching at the Talladega picnic was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Talladega, Alabama, in May 1881, by the father and fellow members of a picnic party who accused him of choking the father's young daughter to death and robbing her. He was hanged to a tree near the falls of a river and his body was left hanging. The story ran across the country as a wire item, often under headlines that approved of the killing, such as 'Justifiable Lynching'.

According to a dispatch from Decatur, a picnic party made an excursion to the falls on a river near Talladega, and among them were Dr. William Toole and his seven-year-old daughter. Her mother had dressed her in gold ornaments and a diamond pin of much value.

Early in the afternoon the father missed the child and searched for her, and near the falls he came upon a man the dispatch called 'a burly negro' carrying her dead body. The papers said the man had enticed the girl away, choked her to death, taken her jewelry, and was about to throw her body into the river or over the falls; these accusations came only from the account of the father and the picnic party. The father fought him for the body, and his cries brought 'a number of the picnic party', who helped overpower the man.

A rope was procured and the man was 'at once strung up to a limb until dead'. The short wire said he was hanged 'by the infuriated mob at the picnic', while the Sacramento copy credited 'her friends and father'. The body was left hanging on the tree, and the picnic party, in the Dallas Weekly Herald's words, 'was changed to a funeral train' that carried the child home to her mother.
No report of an inquest, arrest, or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and no account gives the hanged man's name.

Two versions of the story circulated from May 14, 1881: a short wire dated at Talladega on May 13, relayed through New York, and a longer dispatch from Decatur that named Dr. Toole and described the fight for the body. Headline writers treated the hanging as deserved: the Daily Globe titled it 'Justifiable Lynching' and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union 'Flendish [Fiendish] Murder Promptly Avenged'. The Memphis Daily Appeal used 'Short Shrift and a Stout Rope', and the Chicago Daily Tribune 'Hard on the Tree'. The fuller dispatch called the man 'the fiend' and 'the savage black' and stated the accusation as fact.

Over the following week condensed versions appeared in news columns in Arkansas, Montana and Wisconsin, one of which ended that the man's 'corpse was left to dangle in the wind'. The story was still being reprinted in North Carolina and Pennsylvania weeklies in late May and early June. Later copies drifted in detail, misplacing Talladega in Georgia, giving the girl's age as twelve, and calling the river a pond.

The date is uncertain: the Decatur dispatch of May 13 placed the picnic 'yesterday', the Dallas Weekly Herald said 'Wednesday', and a North Carolina reprint dated the dispatch May 16, which cannot be right for a story already in print on May 14.

reader.title: Lynching at the Talladega picnic (1881)
bases: Every account says a Black man accused of killing a child was seized by her father and members of a picnic party and hanged to a tree without any legal process (A2, A5, A11).

The man was strung up 'until dead' by the father with 'a number of the picnic party' (A2, A11), called 'the infuriated mob at the picnic' (A5), with no officer or court involved, as punishment for the child's alleged murder and robbery (A1, A3).

Two separately datelined dispatches, a Talladega special relayed through New York and wired from Talladega (A3, A4, A5) and a fuller Decatur dispatch (A2, A11), agree that the man was seized at the picnic and hanged to a tree; no local Alabama report, inquest or denial was found.

accounts.label: Talladega wire (short version)
accounts.gist: The girl strayed from the picnic and was choked and robbed by a man caught throwing her body into the river; he was captured after a struggle and hanged to a tree by the men or 'mob' at the picnic, and left hanging.

accounts.label: Decatur dispatch (fuller version)
accounts.gist: Dr. William Toole found a man carrying his seven-year-old daughter's body near the falls, fought him, and with picnic-goers who answered his cries overpowered him and hanged him from a limb; the child had been robbed of her jewels.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Justifiable Lynching' (Daily Globe), 'Fiendish Murder Promptly Avenged' (Sacramento) and 'Short Shrift and a Stout Rope' (Memphis) presented the hanging as deserved punishment.
The fuller dispatch called the man 'the fiend' and 'the savage black' and stated the accusation as fact, with no word of the man's name or side.
Most later copies were condensed news-roundup items repeating the wire.
